articles.headline: Los jabalíes campan a sus anchas por Lugo y los vecinos denuncian la inacción de la Administración
articles.subtitle: Asociaciones vecinales y cazadores alertan de avistamientos diarios en Monte Faro, la Ronda de la Muralla y varias urbanizaciones; Xunta, Deputación y Concello pactaron en agosto un frente común con batidas y desbroces que, denuncian, aún no se ha traducido en medidas sobre el terreno.
articles.body:
Los jabalíes se han convertido en un problema cotidiano en Lugo. Asociaciones vecinales y colectivos de cazadores denuncian que la falta de desbroces empuja a estos animales hasta el casco urbano, con avistamientos a diario en Monte Faro, la Ronda de la Muralla y distintas urbanizaciones de la ciudad, donde revuelven huertas, jardines y contenedores sin que nadie actúe.

La sensación de abandono crece porque el pasado mes de agosto Xunta, Deputación y Concello sellaron un frente común para combatir la proliferación del jabalí, con batidas controladas, prevención y desbroces coordinados, tal y como recogieron entonces La Voz de Galicia y COPE. Un mes después, los vecinos aseguran que ese pacto no se ha traducido en medidas concretas sobre el terreno y que los vallados continúan con agujeros por los que los animales entran en las fincas.

El retraso en los desbroces de las parcelas municipales y privadas es, según las asociaciones, la principal causa de que los jabalíes bajen al monte en busca de comida. Mientras la Administración decide quién actúa, los avistamientos se suceden y crece el temor a accidentes, sobre todo en las zonas próximas a colegios y a la carretera de circunvalación.

articles.headline: Las obras de la Avenida de América en Ribadeo desatan las quejas vecinales por polvo, ruido y cortes de tráfico
articles.subtitle: Los residentes denuncian retenciones de hasta tres kilómetros, falta de información sobre los cortes y el estado de la vía; el BNG habla de descontrol absoluto y exige un plan de movilidad mientras el Concello defiende los plazos de la actuación.
articles.body:
Las obras en la Avenida de América de Ribadeo han convertido el principal acceso a la villa en un quebradero de cabeza para los vecinos. Las quejas se acumulan en redes sociales y en el registro municipal: polvo, ruido, aceras cortadas y cambios de circulación que se comunican con poca antelación, según denuncian los residentes, que llevan semanas viendo cómo se alargan unos trabajos de renovación de la vía.

El BNG de Ribadeo fue más allá y calificó la situación de descontrol absoluto: el portavoz nacionalista denunció retenciones de casi tres kilómetros en el acceso a la localidad durante las horas punta y reclamó al gobierno local un plan de movilidad que ordene los cortes y minimice el impacto sobre el tráfico y el comercio.

El Concello, por su parte, defiende los plazos de la actuación y recuerda que los cambios de circulación ya estaban anunciados desde finales de julio, cuando el gobierno local publicó el plan de desvíos. Mientras tanto, los vecinos piden más información y que las máquinas trabajen en horarios que no afecten al descanso ni a la entrada y salida de los colegios.

articles.headline: Sánchez no asume ningún error sobre Ceuta e irrita a sus socios por exculpar a Marruecos
articles.subtitle: Un mes después de la avalancha, el presidente insiste en que su gestión fue la correcta, atribuye la crisis a una operación rusa y descarta dimisiones; el PSOE muestra su inquietud, Sumar le acusa de autocomplacencia y la oposición exige explicaciones.
articles.body:
Un mes después de la entrada masiva de migrantes en Ceuta, Pedro Sánchez no asume ningún error. En la entrevista concedida este lunes a la Cadena SER, el presidente atribuyó la crisis a una operación de desestabilización auspiciada por Rusia, defendió la gestión de su Gobierno y descartó cualquier dimisión, lo que ha irritado a sus socios de investidura: Sumar, ERC y Podemos le acusan de autocomplacencia y de exculpar a Marruecos, según recoge 20minutos.

La entrevista ha removido además al propio PSOE. El Confidencial asegura que crece la inquietud en el partido y que algunos barones, como el presidente de Castilla-La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, consideran que la comparecencia fue un desastre. El malestar se agrava con las cifras: la ministra de Infancia, Sira Rego, tuvo que corregir al presidente, que habló de miles de menores, cuando en régimen de acogida hay 1.478.

Mientras tanto, El País y El Mundo subrayan la defensa cerrada que Sánchez hizo de Marruecos —al que pidió no tratar como un enemigo— y su promesa de que el Rey visitará Ceuta sin concretar fecha. La oposición, con el PP a la cabeza, exige explicaciones en el Congreso y critica la gestión de la crisis.

articles.headline: Ceuta se queda corta de plazas: el Gobierno anuncia 6.000 cuando miles de migrantes siguen durmiendo en la calle
articles.subtitle: Sánchez avanza que en un muy breve espacio de tiempo habrá 6.000 plazas activas, casi el doble que hace una semana; el Gobierno descarta por ahora el traslado a la península mientras las entidades advierten de que la capacidad sigue siendo insuficiente.
articles.body:
La capacidad de acogida de Ceuta vuelve a estar en el centro del debate. En la entrevista a la Cadena SER, Pedro Sánchez avanzó que en un muy breve espacio de tiempo habrá 6.000 plazas activas para atender a los migrantes que siguen en la ciudad, una cifra que, según elDiario.es, supone casi duplicar en una semana las plazas existentes, que han pasado de 1.800 a 3.300 y que ahora se prevé llevar hasta 6.000.

El Ejecutivo descarta por ahora el traslado de migrantes a la península y trabaja en habilitar nuevos espacios: elDiario.es detalla que unos 500 migrantes ya han sido acogidos en el antiguo almacén de Loma Colmenar y que se prepara el traslado de unos 400 del asentamiento del Príncipe a las instalaciones de La Hípica. La presión, sin embargo, sigue siendo enorme: miles de personas continúan durmiendo a la intemperie mientras se ultiman los centros anunciados.

El anuncio llega en plena tensión con Sumar, cuya ministra, Sira Rego, reclama más recursos y critica la gestión de una crisis en la que el Gobierno ha implantado un mando único. Mientras se habilitan los nuevos espacios, los socios y las entidades sociales advierten de que la capacidad anunciada deberá ir acompañada de recursos suficientes para que sea efectiva.

articles.headline: Las olas de calor dejan 5.232 muertos este verano en España, el peor registro desde que hay datos
articles.subtitle: El sistema MoMo atribuye al calor 5.232 fallecimientos entre junio y agosto, la cifra más alta desde que hay registros; más del 95% eran mayores de 65 años y agosto, con 2.147 muertes, fue el mes más letal de un verano que Aemet certifica como el más cálido desde 1961.
articles.body:
El verano más cálido desde que hay registros deja también la peor factura sanitaria. Según los datos del sistema de monitorización de la mortalidad diaria (MoMo) del Instituto de Salud Carlos III, las olas de calor se cobraron 5.232 muertes entre junio y agosto, la cifra más alta desde que este indicador empezó a computar los fallecimientos atribuibles a las altas temperaturas, superando el anterior máximo de la serie.

El perfil de las víctimas es el de siempre: más del 95% de los fallecidos tenían más de 65 años y 3.256 superaban los 85, según detalla El Mundo. Agosto fue el mes más letal, con 2.147 muertes atribuibles al calor, en un mes marcado por la tercera ola de calor del año, cuando los termómetros superaron los 40 grados en amplias zonas del país.

Los expertos advierten de que el calor extremo es ya una amenaza creciente para la salud pública, un fenómeno que no afecta solo a España. Las autoridades sanitarias insisten en la necesidad de activar los planes de prevención antes de que lleguen las olas y de proteger especialmente a los mayores, los enfermos crónicos y las personas que trabajan al aire libre.

articles.headline: Airbus mantiene la huelga indefinida: el 81% de la plantilla vota seguir mientras la empresa condiciona el acuerdo
articles.subtitle: Los trabajadores rechazan la propuesta de suspender la movilización para negociar; solo Illescas votó a favor de pausarla, y las plantas de Albacete y Cádiz se adhieren a la mayoría; sindicatos y empresa se reúnen mañana en el SIMA.
articles.body:
La huelga indefinida en Airbus España continúa. La plantilla, convocada este lunes a votación para decidir si suspendía temporalmente las movilizaciones para negociar, rechazó la propuesta por un 81,2% de los votos, con solo un 16,4% de respaldo y un 2,4% de abstenciones, según el resultado de las asambleas presenciales, en las que participó cerca de un millar de empleados de los más de 14.000 que el fabricante tiene en España.

Solo la planta de Illescas votó a favor de pausar la movilización, mientras que Albacete y Cádiz, que no votaron, anunciaron que se adhieren al resultado mayoritario. Los sindicatos y la empresa volverán a reunirse mañana en una nueva sesión de mediación en el SIMA, aunque la dirección ha condicionado la continuidad de las negociaciones a la suspensión temporal de la huelga.

Airbus defiende su última oferta, que vincula el salario al IPC real y plantea una recuperación del poder adquisitivo perdido del 7,6% hasta 2030, con un pago excepcional de 2.000 euros en enero de 2027. La compañía advierte de que la continuación de la huelga está creando una situación crítica para su negocio y para sus clientes, mientras los sindicatos aseguran que acudirán mañana al SIMA para ver si la empresa cumple o no sus amenazas.

articles.headline: Deadline passes for Troubles victims' disability compensation after extension refused
articles.subtitle: Applications to the Troubles Permanent Disablement Payment Scheme closed at midnight on Sunday after Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant declined to extend the five-year window; victims' groups say the scheme has become a postcode lottery and that eligible survivors are being left out.
articles.body:
The deadline for applications to the compensation scheme for people permanently disabled during the Troubles passed on Sunday night, after the Government refused calls to extend it. The Troubles Permanent Disablement Payment Scheme, administered by the Victims' Payments Board, opened on 31 August 2021 and closed at midnight, having paid out more than £150 million to applicants as of May this year.

Eligible victims can receive between £2,494 and £12,471 a year. Kenny Donaldson of the South East Fermanagh Foundation said the failure to extend the scheme meant it had ended up as "a postcode lottery", and criticised what he called "a position of delusion by the UK Government" over central funding. Andree Murphy of Relatives For Justice, whose request for an extension was rejected, accused Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant of an "abdication of responsibility" after he said he could not extend the window without a request from the Executive.

Victims' groups say many survivors still have not applied, including those subjected to paramilitary punishment attacks and sexual violence during the conflict, and warn that first-generation victims are dying while they wait. Applications made after the deadline can still be considered by the board in exceptional circumstances.

articles.headline: No Stormont budget is 'catastrophic' for public services, says Pivotal report
articles.subtitle: The think tank's annual review says ministers' failure to agree a budget for the current year, with departments on contingency funding since April, is a serious failing; the Good Jobs Bill and nine other Executive bills have yet to reach the Assembly.
articles.body:
The failure of Stormont ministers to agree a budget is "catastrophic" for public services in Northern Ireland, according to a new report from the Pivotal think tank. Running Out Of Time: The Performance Of The Northern Ireland Executive in 2026 warns that with seven months until the Assembly dissolves, Stormont faces a rush to pass key legislation, including the flagship Good Jobs Bill.

Launching the report, Pivotal director Ann Watt said deciding a budget was "a basic element of good governance" and that the absence of even a single-year budget was "catastrophic". Northern Ireland has not had a multi-year budget in over a decade, and departments have been operating on contingency budgets since April, with projected shortfalls of around £250 million in education and £800 million in health this year.

The report says nine planned Executive bills have yet to be brought before the Assembly, including the 16-18s in Education or Training Bill and the Race Equality Bill, and warns that other flagship goals — the expansion of Magee College, the development of Casement Park and investment in the wastewater system — are at risk. Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald's Good Jobs Bill faces a "race against time" after the DUP said it needs more work.

articles.headline: Boy, 16, charged with murder of Dungannon man found dead beside injured daughter
articles.subtitle: The 16-year-old is due before Omagh Magistrates' Court today after a 61-year-old man was found dead at a house on Lisnahull Road on Saturday; his eight-year-old daughter was seriously injured and his wife also hurt in the attack.
articles.body:
A 16-year-old boy has been charged with the murder of a man in Dungannon, County Tyrone, and the attempted murder of two other people in the same incident. The body of the 61-year-old man was found alongside his seriously injured eight-year-old daughter at a house on Lisnahull Road on Saturday morning, while the man's 48-year-old wife sustained non-life-threatening injuries during the attack.

The teenager has also been charged with making threats to kill and is due to appear before Omagh Magistrates' Court today, having been arrested after the incident at the weekend.

Police have appealed for information from the public as enquiries into the attack continue. Three people were attacked at the property on Saturday, and the wider community has been urged not to speculate about the circumstances while officers piece together what happened.

articles.headline: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur
articles.subtitle: The former South Side Compton Crips leader, 63, was convicted by a Las Vegas jury of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon, the first conviction in the drive-by killing of the rap icon; he faces 20 years to life at sentencing in October.
articles.body:
Duane "Keffe D" Davis, the former South Side Compton Crips leader accused of ordering the 1996 drive-by shooting of rapper Tupac Shakur, has been found guilty of first-degree murder with a deadly weapon by a Las Vegas jury. The verdict, delivered after around two hours of deliberation, is the first conviction in one of hip-hop's most famous cold cases.

Prosecutors argued that Davis orchestrated the attack on 7 September 1996, in which Shakur was shot multiple times in a car on the Las Vegas Strip and died six days later at the age of 25. Key evidence included Davis's own admissions in a 2008 interview and in his memoir, in which he described being in the car from which the shots were fired and supplying the gun to his nephew, Orlando Anderson.

Davis, 63, showed little reaction as the verdict was read. The judge set sentencing for October, where he faces 20 years to life in prison. His lawyers have said they will appeal, arguing the case relied too heavily on Davis's own statements.

articles.headline: Nepal rescuers blast hillside to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels
articles.subtitle: The death toll from the Nepal-Tibet floods has risen to 939 with 3,925 people missing, as crews drill and blast through debris to reach more than 600 workers trapped after flash floods hit hydropower projects; Tibet reports 16 dead.
articles.body:
Rescuers in Nepal are drilling and blasting through a hillside in a desperate bid to reach more than 600 workers feared trapped in tunnels at two hydropower projects, after flash floods triggered by heavy rain swept through the region last week.

The official death toll from the disaster has risen to 939, with 3,925 people still missing, and Nepal's government has faced criticism over the scale of the destruction. In Tibet, authorities report at least 16 dead and 546 missing, while censorship of independent reporting in the region has complicated efforts to establish the full picture, according to the BBC and The Guardian.

Families of the trapped workers have gathered at the sites, waiting anxiously as crews work around the clock. In Chitwan, hundreds of bodies have been cremated at a temporary site as the country begins to count the cost of what is already among the deadliest natural disasters in Nepal's recent history.

articles.headline: Shein shares slide on Hong Kong debut as $26bn valuation marks a dramatic fall from its peak
articles.subtitle: The fast-fashion giant priced at HK$48.56, raising HK$13.6bn, but shares slipped on the first day of trading; the listing values the company at US$26.3bn, a fraction of the US$98bn it was worth before its abandoned 2024 IPO.
articles.body:
Shein made its long-awaited stock market debut in Hong Kong on Tuesday, and the shares slid. The fast-fashion giant, which serves more than 270 million customers, priced its initial public offering at HK$48.56, raising around HK$13.6 billion in what is Hong Kong's largest listing this year, but the stock fell on its first day of trading.

The listing values Shein at about US$26.3 billion — a dramatic fall from the US$98.2 billion peak valuation it commanded in 2022, before its planned 2024 IPO in New York was abandoned amid regulatory scrutiny in Washington and questions over its supply chain practices.

Analysts cited persistent concerns about trade tariffs, the company's reliance on Chinese manufacturing, and regulatory risk in both the US and Europe. With its market valuation well below the earlier peak and rivals such as Temu owner PDD trading at higher multiples, investors remain cautious about the company's growth prospects outside China.

articles.headline: UN committee says countries are legally obliged to consider slavery reparations
articles.subtitle: In new guidance, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination says states have a legal duty to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and its legacies, including compensation, restitution and official apologies.
articles.body:
Countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and its ongoing legacies, according to new guidance from the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination. The committee said the duty flows from the 1965 International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to address the historical injustices that continue to drive inequality.

The guidance urges states to consider a range of measures, including financial compensation, restitution of assets, formal apologies, education programmes and other forms of redress, and says the obligation is not merely moral but legal. The committee's interpretation is expected to add momentum to the global reparations debate, which has gained ground in Caribbean nations and among African and European governments.

Campaigners welcomed the clarification, saying it gives legal weight to demands that have often been dismissed as symbolic. The guidance comes as several countries and institutions, including the UK, continue to face pressure over their historical involvement in the slave trade, with the committee urging states to consult affected communities in designing any measures.

articles.headline: FTC and 21 states sue Amazon over 'secret' ad surcharge scheme
articles.subtitle: The FTC alleges Amazon raised prices for Sponsored Products advertisers through a hidden 'soft reserve price' auction system, potentially reaping tens of billions of dollars; Amazon denies the claims, calling the lawsuit 'meritless'.
articles.body:
The US Federal Trade Commission and 21 states filed suit against Amazon on Monday, alleging the company secretly raised prices for advertisers on its Sponsored Products platform. According to the complaint, Amazon ran a hidden 'soft reserve price' system that pushed up the minimum bid advertisers had to pay without telling them, in what the agency describes as a covert scheme that may have reaped tens of billions of dollars from sellers.

The lawsuit asks the court to order Amazon to stop the alleged scheme and to pay damages. New Jersey's attorney general is among the 21 state officials who joined the federal action, which follows an investigation into the company's advertising business.

Amazon called the lawsuit meritless, saying its advertising products are optional tools that have helped small businesses reach customers, and that the FTC's claims mischaracterise how its auction system works. The company said it will defend itself in court. The case adds to a long list of antitrust and consumer-protection battles between the agency and the e-commerce giant.

articles.headline: Polymarket raises $300m from Donald Trump Jr.'s investment fund, report says
articles.subtitle: The prediction-market platform is reportedly close to a $300 million investment from 1789 Capital, the fund co-founded by Donald Trump Jr., as US states and regulators push back against election betting and its rivals face legal pressure.
articles.body:
Polymarket is reportedly raising $300 million from 1789 Capital, the investment fund co-founded by Donald Trump Jr., in a deal first reported by the Wall Street Journal. The round would value the prediction-market platform at a time when election betting in the US is under intense regulatory scrutiny from state attorneys general, the White House and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The investment arrives as the platform's main rivals come under legal attack: New York and several other states have sued Kalshi and Polymarket over election contracts, arguing the markets violate state gaming law and undermine public confidence in elections. Regulators in Washington have also signalled a crackdown on the industry's rapid growth.

Polymarket has said little publicly about the reported round. The platform became a major player during recent US election cycles, processing billions of dollars in wagers, and has repeatedly insisted it operates lawfully. Supporters of prediction markets say they improve forecasting; critics counter that they invite manipulation and gambling-style behaviour around democratic processes.

articles.headline: ChatGPT ads hit $1bn annualised run rate as self-serve platform expands to Europe
articles.subtitle: OpenAI says advertisers have generated $1 billion in annualised revenue in under 200 days and is rolling out its self-serve Ads Manager across India, Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, opening the platform to SMBs in more than 40 countries.
articles.body:
OpenAI's advertising business has reached a $1 billion annualised revenue run rate in less than 200 days, the company announced, as it expands the self-serve version of its Ads Manager to India, Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. OpenAI says tens of thousands of advertisers have bought ChatGPT ads so far, and that small and medium businesses now make up a material share of spend.

Most campaigns now use cost-per-click or outcome-optimised bidding rather than the flat CPMs of the early pilot, according to the company, which launched ads inside ChatGPT in the US earlier this year and has been expanding market by market. The European rollout began in late August across 31 markets, with brands from the Cannes Lions summer festival among the first wave.

Advertisers have responded to the platform's reach: ChatGPT now serves roughly 900 million weekly users, and industry analysts see the ads business as a key pillar of OpenAI's long-term revenue plans alongside consumer subscriptions and API access. The company has set out ambitions to build a multi-billion-dollar advertising franchise over the next few years, while promising to keep sponsored messages clearly labelled.

articles.headline: Instagram slashes reach of undisclosed AI-generated profiles
articles.subtitle: Following Wired's investigation into AI influencers, Meta renamed the 'AI creator' label to 'AI-generated profile' and is now reducing the visibility and monetisation of accounts that don't use it; creators can appeal via Account Status.
articles.body:
Instagram is cracking down on AI-generated accounts that do not disclose their synthetic nature. The platform has renamed its 'AI creator' label to 'AI-generated profile' and will now reduce the reach of accounts that publish AI content without the label, making them non-recommendable across Reels, Explore and other surfaces, and limiting their ability to earn from monetisation.

The move, announced on Monday, follows a Wired investigation into AI influencers and the rapid spread of synthetic creator accounts on the platform. It also lands as Meta works through a wave of regulatory pressure around transparency and online safety, and days after the company agreed to a multibillion-dollar settlement over alleged ad-fraud practices.

Creators who believe their account was mislabelled can appeal through Instagram's Account Status tool. The changes apply to new content going forward, and Instagram says it will keep refining the policy as detection improves. The company has not said how it will police accounts that deliberately hide their AI nature, beyond the reach penalty and label enforcement.

articles.headline: OpenClaw 2.0 lands with multiplayer sessions and stronger security for enterprise agents
articles.subtitle: The open-source AI assistant framework's biggest release adds shared cloud sessions, a redesigned Control UI and security features including sandboxing, role-based access and a Secret Store, as the project's foundation prepares for corporate adoption.
articles.body:
OpenClaw, the open-source AI assistant framework, shipped its 2.0 release this week, the project's biggest update since its rapid rise out of the Claude Code ecosystem. Version 2026.8.1 introduces multiplayer sessions, shared cloud sessions and a redesigned Control UI, letting teams run and observe AI agents collaboratively rather than as isolated single-user processes.

The release also puts security front and centre for enterprise use: sandboxing, role-based access control, approval workflows and a Secret Store for credentials, all designed to make agent deployments auditable and safe. The project says it has grown to more than 900 contributors and 16,000 pull requests, and is now governed by the OpenClaw Foundation, a non-profit set up to steer development and licensing.

The 2.0 milestone arrives as enterprises increasingly standardise on open agent frameworks, and as its lead maintainer, Peter Steinberger, now works with OpenAI on agent tooling. The team describes the release as deliberately conservative on defaults, prioritising stability and security over raw capability, with the full changelog published on the project's documentation site.
